title: Linking CSS, JS & Favicons
summary: A favicon is the small icon a browser shows for a website or page.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: A `<link>` element in the document head can point to a favicon file. It does not appear as a visible control in the page body. It is like attaching a label to the folder rather than printing it inside the document. Make sure the path works after the site is deployed. For example, verify the icon path on a nested route, not just at the site root.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: The `rel` attribute describes the relationship between the current page and the linked resource. For an icon, use the appropriate icon relationship. It is like labeling a package as a logo or stylesheet. The browser uses this hint to decide how to interpret the linked file. For example, a simplified mark remains clearer in a tab than a detailed full logo.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: A favicon should remain recognizable when shown very small. A detailed logo may become an unreadable blur. It is like simplifying a road sign so drivers can identify it quickly. Use a simple mark, check light and dark browser themes, and provide formats and sizes supported by your deployment needs. For example, check a light and dark tab background when selecting icon contrast.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: Use a stable file path and verify that the icon returns successfully from the deployed site. A correct local path can still break when an app is hosted beneath a subpath. It is like checking the street address after moving offices. Inspect the browser tab and network response after deployment. For example, a missing icon should not prevent page content and controls from working.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: A missing favicon should not prevent the page from loading or working. It is a helpful identity detail, not the content itself. It is like a missing folder sticker: inconvenient, but the papers are still available. Keep the HTML valid and prioritize accessible, functional page content first. For example, use the appropriate link relationship so the browser recognizes the resource.

foundations.overview: A favicon is a small icon associated with a website. Browsers may show it in tabs, bookmarks, history, or mobile shortcuts. HTML links the file from the document head using a `<link>` element. Think of it like a small label on a folder. Keep it recognizable at tiny sizes and treat it as polish rather than required page content.
foundations.whyItMatters: Favicons improve recognition in browser chrome and saved shortcuts. They are useful polish, while core document content and accessibility remain higher priorities.
foundations.browserPerspective: While parsing HTML, the browser's preload scanner spots <link> and <script> tags and starts fetching them in parallel. CSS blocks the first paint; a plain <script> blocks the parser; defer/async let parsing continue. Hints like preconnect/preload reorder and prioritize these fetches.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every site links a stylesheet, a bundle of JS (usually deferred or as a module), and a set of favicons. Performance-focused sites add preconnect to font/CDN origins and preload critical fonts or hero images. Build tools (Vite, webpack) inject these tags automatically.
foundations.businessImpact: Load speed affects bounce rate, conversions, and SEO (Core Web Vitals). Render-blocking scripts and missing resource hints slow first paint; getting linking right keeps pages fast, which retains users.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding defer/async and hint semantics lets engineers debug slow loads, eliminate flashes of unstyled/un-fonted content, and order critical resources correctly — often the difference between a janky and a smooth load.
foundations.performanceImpact: This is largely a performance topic: CSS placement controls first paint, defer/async control parser blocking and execution order, and preconnect/preload/dns-prefetch shave latency off critical-path fetches.
commonUseCases: <link rel=stylesheet> in the head for site CSS
<script defer> in the head for app code that needs the DOM
<script async> for independent third-party scripts like analytics
Favicon + apple-touch-icon set for tabs and iOS bookmarks
preconnect to a font host and preload of a critical font/hero image

commonMisconceptions.myth: async and defer are basically the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Both download in parallel without blocking parsing, but defer runs after parsing in document order, while async runs as soon as it loads, in unpredictable order. Use defer for ordered app code, async for independent scripts.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must put all <script> tags at the end of <body>.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That was the workaround before defer existed. Today a <script defer> in the head downloads in parallel and runs after parsing — cleaner and just as non-blocking.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You always need a favicon.ico file.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Browsers auto-request /favicon.ico, but a modern <link rel="icon"> pointing to an SVG or PNG works fine and scales better; .ico is optional legacy support.

visualExplorer.title: How the browser loads linked resources
visualExplorer.caption: Watch the page load step by step — see where CSS blocks paint and how defer keeps the parser moving.

config.intro: As the browser reads HTML top to bottom, it discovers linked resources and decides what blocks and what loads in the background.

steps.name: Parse <head>
steps.detail: The browser reads the head and discovers <link> and <script> tags, kicking off parallel downloads via the preload scanner.

steps.name: Block on CSS
steps.detail: Render-blocking <link rel=stylesheet> must arrive before the first paint, so the browser holds painting to avoid unstyled flashes.

steps.name: Defer scripts
steps.detail: A <script defer> downloads in parallel but does not run yet; HTML parsing continues uninterrupted.

steps.name: Apply resource hints
steps.detail: preconnect opens early connections; preload fetches high-priority assets (font, hero image) ahead of need.

steps.name: Finish parsing & run deferred JS
steps.detail: After the DOM is built, deferred scripts execute in document order, then DOMContentLoaded fires.

steps.name: Fetch favicon
steps.detail: The browser requests the icon from <link rel=icon> (or /favicon.ico) to show in the tab.

interactiveExamples.title: Linking CSS and a deferred script
interactiveExamples.explanation: The stylesheet is in the head so styles load before paint; the script uses defer so it runs after the DOM is ready and can safely touch elements.

files.index.html:
Loading…

CSS is in the head; JS is deferred.
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 24px; }
h1 { color: #2563eb; }

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A styled page whose heading reads 'Loaded after parsing!' because the deferred script ran once the DOM was ready.

interactiveExamples.title: ES module + resource hints
interactiveExamples.explanation: type="module" enables import/export and is deferred by default. A preconnect hint warms up a connection to a font origin so it's ready when CSS requests the font.

files.index.html: …
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 24px; }
h1 { color: #16a34a; }
files.main.mjs:
const greet = (n) => `Hello from a module, ${n}!`;
document.getElementById('out').textContent = greet('world');

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The heading shows 'Hello from a module, world!', set by the ES module which runs deferred.

codeLab.title: Wire up CSS, a deferred script, and a favicon
codeLab.instructions: This page has inline styles and a render-blocking script in the body. Move the CSS link into the head, add a deferred external script reference to app.js, and add a favicon link. Keep the page working.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 24px; }
h1 { color: #7c3aed; }

codeLab.expectedOutput: A styled page whose heading reads 'Set by deferred app.js', with a favicon link in the head.

hints: The stylesheet link goes in the head; the script uses src + defer so it runs after the DOM is parsed.
A favicon is a <link rel="icon"> in the head.

keyTakeaways: A `<link>` element in the document head can point to a favicon file.
The `rel` attribute describes the relationship between the current page and the linked resource.
A favicon should remain recognizable when shown very small.
Use a stable file path and verify that the icon returns successfully from the deployed site.
A missing favicon should not prevent the page from loading or working.
